title: Supermicrosurgical perforator-to-perforator flap reconstruction for lower limb defects: a single-center case series.
abstract: Lower limb soft tissue defects remain a major reconstructive challenge due to frequent exposure of critical structures and compromised vascularity. In complex cases where local tissue is insufficient, free tissue transfer is required. Advances in supermicrosurgery have enabled perforator-to-perforator (P-to-P) anastomoses allowing reliable perfusion while preserving major axial vessels and minimizing donor-site morbidity. A retrospective review was conducted of five patients who underwent P-to-P free flap reconstruction for lower limb defects between January 2018 and January 2023. Preoperative CT angiography and intraoperative duplex ultrasound were used for perforator mapping. Two anterolateral thigh, one medial sural artery perforator, and two gracilis muscle flaps were utilized. Anastomoses were hand-sewn using 10-0 to 12-0 nylon under high-magnification microscopy. Flap perfusion was monitored with Vioptix Tissue Oximeter. The mean age was 60.8 years and defect sizes ranged from 5 × 4 cm to 20 × 8 cm. All flaps survived without partial or total loss. One patient developed minor wound dehiscence that healed without intervention. Reconstruction was successful across varied etiologies including infection, chronic wounds, and postoperative defects, with low morbidity and no re-explorations. P-to-P supermicrosurgical reconstruction offers a reliable, vessel-preserving approach for complex lower limb defects. This technique maintains major vascular axes, minimizes donor-site morbidity, and achieves outcomes comparable to conventional microsurgical methods across diverse etiologies such as infection, chronic wounds, and postoperative defects. In our series, flap survival was universal with no re-explorations and minimal morbidity. Wider clinical adoption and continued experience may further define its role in contemporary lower extremity reconstruction.

title: CT image-based evaluation of phantom-derived DLP-to-effective dose conversion factors for adult abdomen-pelvis CT.
abstract: Effective dose is used in computed tomography (CT) as a population-level quantity for radiation protection, dose monitoring, and clinical studies. It is commonly estimated by multiplying scanner-reported dose-length product (DLP) by a conversion coefficient, or k -factor, because organ doses are not available from routine examinations. Most CT k -factors were derived from computational human phantoms, but phantom-derived estimates have not been systematically compared with effective doses calculated directly from CT images across adults with diverse body habitus. We calculated k -factors using a set of adult abdominal CT images combined with deep learning-based automatic organ segmentation and Monte Carlo dose calculation methods and compared them with those calculated from two phantom-derived k -factor approaches: the fixed AAPM TG23 coefficient and body size-dependent k -factors calculated using National Cancer Institute dosimetry system for CT (NCICT). Abdomen-pelvis CT images from 38 adults (18 females, 20 males) spanning water-equivalent diameter (WED) values of 21-41 cm were segmented using TotalSegmentator and an in-house gonad model, converted into voxelised anatomical models, and coupled with a validated CT scanner Monte Carlo model. CT image-based k -factors were calculated as effective dose divided by DLP and evaluated as functions of WED and sex. Image-based k -factors decreased with increasing WED for both sexes, and female values were higher than male values at comparable WED. Over the overlapping WED range, NCICT-based k -factors showed good agreement with CT-based values with the same decreasing trend. The fixed TG23 coefficient introduced systematic bias at smaller and larger body sizes. However, the selected NCICT adult phantoms did not cover the lower-WED end of the CT cohort. These findings support the performance of phantom-based effective dose calculations and indicate the need to extend phantom libraries while continuing CT image-based evaluation across pediatric CT and broader imaging protocols.

title: Determination of local diagnostic reference levels for mammography in Fars Province, Iran.
abstract: The most common cancer that strikes women is breast cancer. It is diagnosed using mammography, which is considered a gold standard diagnostic tool in detecting breast cancer. Despite the use of ionizing radiation, mammography should be performed according to the ALARA principle, ensuring that radiation dose is optimized while maintaining adequate image quality for accurate diagnosis. This study sought to determine the LDRL for mammography in Fars Province, Iran, in line with the guidelines provided in ICRP Publication 135. This analytical study involved the extraction of data from the DICOM header of quality-controlled mammography devices in 62 centers in Fars Province. In total, 27,345 mammogram reports ranging from 2004 to 2025 were analyzed. Technical information about mammography was obtained through kVp, mAs, anode filter combination, and patient information, including age and compressed breast thickness. Data from the past five years and projections of CC and MLO were considered in the analysis.The study determined LDRLs for both Entrance Surface Air Kerma (Kae) and organ dose. For Kae, which does not require breast thickness correction, the LDRL was established at 5.94 mGy for the CC view and 9.49 mGy for the MLO view. The LDRLs for organ dose were further stratified by breast thickness. A comparison with national and international standards revealed that while the LDRL for the CC view was lower than the NDRLs of the UK and Ireland, it remained higher than previously reported levels in Iran. Notably, the LDRL for the MLO view was found to be higher than levels reported in other Iranian studies and international benchmarks. These findings highlight the necessity for protocol optimization, particularly for the MLO view, to align local practices with global dose reduction standards.

title: MPISuperRes-PnP: a super-resolution zero-shot plug-and-play reconstruction algorithm for magnetic particle imaging.
abstract: Objective. Magnetic particle imaging (MPI) is a promising, emerging medical imaging modality. MPI is based on the non-linear response of magnetic nanoparticles to an applied magnetic field and does not expose the specimen to ionizing radiation. The measured signal is the voltage induced in receive coils by the particles' response. Reconstructing the particle concentration from the signal constitutes the imaging task. Even using state-of-the-art measurement-based reconstruction, the associated spatial grid is very coarse, hence super-resolution techniques are important. In this work, we propose an approach for super-resolution in MPI inspired by energy minimization. Approach. Different methods have been proposed for super-resolution in MPI, ranging from upscaling of the associated system matrix to interpolation of the reconstruction. Here we incorporate super-resolution into the reconstruction task via an energy minimization formulation. Following the plug-and-play (PnP) approach to energy minimization we derive a splitting scheme where the arising Gaussian denoising task is treated with a pre-trained learned Gaussian denoiser. Main results. We derive a super-resolution method for MPI based on a PnP approach using a pre-trained denoiser in zero-shot fashion. This way, we incorporate benefits of deep learning without training and avoid the need of training data. Further, we provide a quantitative and qualitative evaluation of the proposed method on simulated data with realistic noise. Hyper-parameters are selected via an extended parameter search. The found parameters are applied for reconstruction on real data. We qualitatively show the applicability of our method on real data (MPIData: EquilibriumModelWithAnisotropy and 2D-OpenMPI Data). Significance. The proposed method employs a deep-learning denoiser without training-thus it does not require presently scarcely available MPI training data. The denoiser behaves conservatively, i.e. no hallucination artifacts were observed. The super-resolution approach is generic such that it can be applied in future MPI contexts involving different regularizers or different imaging tasks.

title: GPT-assisted radiomic modeling for predicting pathological complete response to neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
abstract: Objective . To evaluate whether GPT can assist in automating radiomics modeling for predicting pathological complete response to neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. Methods. The study included a training cohort (TC; n = 186), a validation cohort (VC; n = 116), and a prospective multicenter validation cohort (PVC; n = 269). Radiomic and supervised deep learning features were extracted from pretreatment T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging. logistic regression (LR) was first evaluated using radiomic, deep learning, and fused features. Support vector machine, naïve Bayes, random forest, and extreme gradient boosting models were subsequently compared using fused features. GPT was not used as the classifier but assisted with preprocessing, feature selection, hyperparameter optimization, code generation and execution, model training, and probability output. Each GPT-assisted workflow was independently repeated five times. Results. Fused features achieved the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve for both manually developed and GPT-assisted LR models. Their AUCs were 0.759 versus 0.763 ± 0.003 in the TC, 0.714 versus 0.741 ± 0.008 in the VC, and 0.700 versus 0.706 ± 0.004 in the PVC. Across five classifiers, GPT-assisted workflows achieved performance broadly comparable to manually developed models. Repeated GPT-assisted runs showed limited variability, with AUC standard deviations ranging from 0.001 to 0.019. Conclusion. Under expert supervision, GPT can automate key radiomics modeling procedures while achieving performance comparable to conventional machine learning workflows, potentially reducing technical workload and facilitating integrated model development.

title: NHPVS: a nodule-aware deep learning method for high-abundance pulmonary vessel segmentation on chest CT.
abstract: Objective. Deep learning-based segmentation of pulmonary vessels is challenged by vessel-nodule confusion and insufficient detection of small vessels. To address these issues, we propose a Nodule-aware High-abundance Pulmonary Vessel Segmentation (NHPVS) framework that enhances nodule differentiation and improves small vessel segmentation. Approach. This multi-center study retrospectively collected 477 chest CT scans comprising non-contrast and contrast scans. A 3D U-Net-based model was trained on 370 scans for pulmonary vessel segmentation. Performance metrics included Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), sensitivity, centerline DSC (cl DSC), 95% Hausdorff distance (HD95), and nodule misclassification rate (NMR). Visual and quantitative assessments were conducted on the external test set. Main Results. NHPVS outperformed existing methods, achieving a DSC of 89.2%, a sensitivity of 89.2%, a cl DSC of 93.2%, an HD95 of 1.4 mm, and an NMR of 1.8%. Compared with the state-of-the-art method (nnUNet-v2), NHPVS showed superior segmentation accuracy, vascular continuity, and branch abundance, with improvements of 31.1% in vessel length and 60.5% in branch counts. The volume of small pulmonary vessels (diameter <3 mm) segmented by NHPVS was significantly greater than that segmented by nnUNet-v2 ( p < 0.001). Significance. By enabling the precise visualization of pulmonary arteries and veins on chest CT, NHPVS has the potential to assist radiologists in disease diagnosis and surgical planning.

Visual and quantitative assessments were conducted on the external test set.Main Results.NHPVS outperformed existing methods, achieving a DSC of 89.2%, a sensitivity of 89.2%, a cl DSC of 93.2%, an HD95 of 1.4 mm, and an NMR of 1.8%. Compared with the state-of-the-art method (nnUNet-v2), NHPVS showed superior segmentation accuracy, vascular continuity, and branch abundance, with improvements of 31.1% in vessel length and 60.5% in branch counts. The volume of small pulmonary vessels (diameter <3 mm) segmented by NHPVS was significantly greater than that segmented by nnUNet-v2 (p< 0.001).Significance.By enabling the precise visualization of pulmonary arteries and veins on chest CT, NHPVS has the potential to assist radiologists in disease diagnosis and surgical planning.

title: Pulse width-dependent Monte Carlo source modeling for ultra-high dose rate electron beams.
abstract: Objective. The emergence of ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) electron beams has highlighted the need for accurate Monte Carlo (MC) source models after recent measurements revealed pulse width (PW)-dependent discrepancies in dose profiles. This work aims to develop and validate a MC source model for conventional and FLASH modes using GATE 10, including PW dependence. Approach. Percentage depth dose (PDD) curves and lateral dose profiles were measured in water using a flashDiamond detector for PWs of 0.5-5s. These data were used to optimize the parametric source model throughminimization and gamma analysis. Validation was performed using a mouse collimator and PMMA slabs. Relative dose distributions and cumulative dose-volume histograms were computed in a CT-based voxelised mouse, with and without bolus. Main results. The optimized FLASH source model features a dual-peak energy spectrum with a PW-dependent energy component (7.0-7.8 MeV for 0.5-5s) and low-energy component probability. In conventional mode, a two-component spectrum (1.51.0 and 6.81.5 MeV) was used. Simulations showed good agreement with measurements (gamma-index 2 mm/2% anddifferences for,and). Differences in the mouse lung volume receiving at least 95% of the maximum dose (V95) were 1% across FLASH PWs, increasing to 5% and 12% in CONV without and with bolus, respectively. Bolus increased V95in FLASH by 17%, indicating improved target coverage. Significance. A GATE 10 MC-based source model of the ElectronFLASH LINAC was developed for both UHDR (PW-dependent) and conventional modes. Despite PW-dependent energy variations, no significant dosimetric differences were observed between PWs in FLASH in the preclinical mouse model. The model provides a reliable tool for optimization of preclinical irradiation setups for FLASH biological studies in the absence of a treatment planning system.

title: Anatomy-prior-guided and scan-aware 3D segmentation of the pediatric pancreas in CT images.
abstract: Objective. Pediatric pancreas CT segmentation is challenging because developmental anatomy and scan-protocol variability jointly affect organ size, image appearance, and boundary visibility. This study evaluated whether explicitly incorporating anatomy-related and scan-related case-level descriptors could improve pediatric pancreas segmentation relative to an image-only baseline. Approach. We developed APSC-Net, an anatomy-prior-guided and scan-aware 3D segmentation framework based on SegResNet. Structured anatomy-related and scan-related descriptors were encoded as separate context vectors and injected through bottleneck anatomy-prior guidance and decoder-stage low-rank FiLM modulation. The model was trained and internally tested on GE pediatric CT cases, then evaluated without retraining on a held-out Siemens subset in a cross-vendor evaluation within the same cohort and institution. Main results. On the full held-out GE test set, APSC-Net improved the mean dice similarity coefficient (DSC) from 0.665 to 0.770 and reduced the 95% Hausdorff distance (HD95) from 22.2 to 11.6 mm compared with an image-only SegResNet baseline. Stratified analysis showed DSC gains across pediatric age groups, including the youngest subgroup (0.718-0.751 for 0-5 years), and across exposure-stage strata. In the GE stream ablation, the full and scan-only configurations performed similarly. In secondary testing on held-out Siemens cases, the full model achieved lower average symmetric surface distance (ASSD) than either single-stream variant and achieved the lowest HD95 and ASSD among the compared methods, while age-group domain-regularized baselines remained competitive in DSC. Significance. On the evaluated cohorts, APSC-Net achieved lower boundary-distance errors than the image-only SegResNet baseline. The findings support further evaluation of case-level metadata conditioning for pediatric imaging tasks affected by developmental and acquisition-related variability.

title: Deep learning-based prediction of diffusion MRI responses from microvascular OCT angiograms.
abstract: Objective. Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) signals are sensitive to microvascular geometry and hemodynamics, but current approaches rely on computationally intensive simulations on optical coherence tomography (OCT)-derived vascular graphs. We investigated whether three-dimensional deep learning models can serve as fast surrogates that predict diffusion MRI responses directly from microvascular OCT angiograms. Approach. Five mouse cortical OCT angiograms were segmented into 4792 vascular subgraphs and converted into nine-channel image volumes encoding vascular geometry, magnetic field gradient, hematocrit, oxygen saturation, partial oxygen pressure, blood velocity magnitude, and three velocity components. For each sample, a physics-based framework generated spin echo (SE) and diffusion-weighted signals for three-values (50, 100, 500 s mm), three gradient timing pairs, and ten gradient directions. We trained five 3D architectures (AutoEncoder, BasicUNet, DenseNet169, EfficientNetB4 and ResNet) with late fusion of acquisition parameters and evaluated performance using MSE, MAE and. Main results. Under within-distribution (random-split) evaluation, testvalues were at least 0.87. DenseNet169 achieved the best overall accuracy (MSE, MAE,) and maintainedacross all diffusion settings, while ResNet provided near-perfect reconstruction of the SE sequence alone (). Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation gave MSE, MAE, and, with 34.4% of held-out samples reaching. Channel ablation revealed velocity magnitude and velocity components as dominant predictors. Once trained, the models predicted full diffusion responses in milliseconds, providing speedups of four to six orders of magnitude compared with simulations. Significance. These results demonstrate that deep learning surrogates can accurately and efficiently approximate diffusion MRI responses from microvascular OCT angiograms, enabling rapid exploration of microvascular configurations and acquisition protocols.

title: DiffINR: conditional neural field diffusion for deformation-driven volumetric image estimation from limited measurements.
abstract: Objective. We propose DiffINR for rapid deformation-driven estimation of patient-specific target volumes from limited measurements. DiffINR uses a coordinate-based implicit neural representation (INR) to estimate a dense deformation vector field (DVF) that warps a high-quality prior volume (source) to the target anatomy, with patient-specific INR initialization provided by a population-based conditional hyperdiffusion model. Approach. During offline training, INRs were optimized on fully sampled source-target image volume pairs to represent DVFs. A Transformer diffusion model, hyperdiffusion, learned the distribution of the resulting INR weights. The model was jointly conditioned on anatomical features extracted from the training source and target volumes by a foundation model and on features encoded directly from limited measurements. At inference, hyperdiffusion generated INR initial weights, which were further fine-tuned by patient-specific optimization using measurement-domain fidelity and DVF-smoothness losses. We evaluated DiffINR on two tasks: cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) estimation from limited-angle x-ray projections and real-time volumetric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) estimation from ultra-sparse k-space data. Main Results. For orthogonal-view 90° CBCT estimation, DiffINR achieved a structural similarity index measure (SSIM) of 0.962 ± 0.021, relative error of 6.84% ± 1.70%, and target registration error of 3.61 ± 1.27 mm, outperforming the iterative methods, population-based models, and randomly initialized INR baselines. For volumetric MRI estimation with 13 radial spokes per slice, DiffINR achieved an SSIM of 0.985 ± 0.007, Dice coefficient of 0.89 ± 0.04, and center-of-mass error of 1.30 ± 1.09 mm. DiffINR showed high robustness to data distribution shifts at test time, including dataset changes, limited-angle setting variations, and different MRI sampling sparsity levels. Test-time runtime was 23 s for CBCT estimation and 27 s for MRI estimation, compared with 795 s and 928 s, respectively, for INR optimization from scratch. Significance. By combining hyperdiffusion-based INR initialization with patient-specific data consistency, DiffINR achieves fast and accurate deformation-driven volumetric image estimation.

title: Characterizing magnetic field coupling in MRI-guided radiotherapy by solving a dirichlet problem with sparsely sampled boundary conditions.
abstract: Objective. Integrating medical linear accelerators and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanners for MRI-guided radiotherapy (MRgRT) is complicated by mutual magnetic field coupling, making efficient field mapping crucial. This study proposes a computationally efficient methodology to characterize an MR scanner's magnetic fringe field by solving a boundary value problem (BVP) from sparsely sampled data. This approach accurately maps fields in free space and near ferromagnetic materials without requiring proprietary internal MR coil models or full-scale room simulations. Approach. A full-scale finite element method (FEM) model of a proximity-type MRgRT system, validated against experimental measurements, was used as the reference. A hybrid BVP methodology was developed where Laplace's equation was first solved using sparsely sampled magnetic field boundary conditions. To account for the linac, this free-space solution was subsequently used as an initial condition for a refined model that incorporated the ferromagnetic properties of the linac head and was solved using Maxwell's equations. Accuracy was assessed by comparing the BVP solutions to the full-scale FEM reference across various sampling resolutions. Main results. The BVP approach reconstructed the magnetic field to within 1 G of the reference using a coarse 40 cm boundary sampling. The hybrid method successfully characterized field distortions from the linac; ignoring the ferromagnetic structure led to errors of -7 G to 2 G near the component, whereas including it reduced the discrepancy to within 1 G. The methodology was efficient, reducing computation time from 2 h for the full-scale model to under 10 min, while using a fraction of the memory. Significance. This study presents a validated, efficient, and accessible BVP-based methodology for magnetic field characterization in MRgRT systems. By enabling accurate field mapping from sparse data, accounting for ferromagnetic components, and drastically reducing computational demands, this approach offers a robust tool for rapid engineering assessments and serves as a practical alternative to complex full-scale simulations.

title: Multi-GPU parallel framework for DOI-enabled long axial field-of-view PET image reconstruction.
abstract: Objective. Depth-of-interaction (DOI)-enabled long axial field-of-view (LAFOV) positron emission tomography (PET) can mitigate parallax-induced resolution degradation, but DOI modeling substantially expands the lines-of-response space and increases computational cost. This study aimed to develop a scalable reconstruction framework for DOI-enabled LAFOV-PET. Approach. We present an optimized multi-GPU reconstruction framework based on list-mode ordered-subsets expectation maximization. The framework targets the major computational bottlenecks of DOI-enabled LAFOV-PET reconstruction, including sensitivity image calculation and Monte Carlo-based scatter estimation. Main results. The extended IQ phantom demonstrated near-linear scalability across multiple GPUs for sensitivity image calculation and Monte Carlo-based scatter estimation. Additional Derenzo and hybrid anthropomorphic phantom studies validated the imaging benefits of DOI modeling, including improved spatial resolution and performance under realistic imaging conditions. Significance. The proposed framework improves the scalability of DOI-enabled LAFOV-PET reconstruction by enabling its dominant computational components to efficiently utilize available GPU resources, establishing a foundation for high-performance reconstruction in next-generation PET systems.

title: Applying exponential data consistency conditions to non-homogeneous attenuation.
abstract: Objective. Exponential data consistency conditions (eDCCs) have shown feasibility for motion correction and attenuation map alignment in single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT). The eDCCs require all the activity to be contained within a convex region of homogeneous attenuation. In a non-homogeneous attenuation, activity outside the convex region can violate this assumption, introducing an additional source of inconsistency and inhibiting eDCC-based methods. We present the mathematical foundations of the sine-amplitude approach for coping with activity outside the region of constant attenuation and validate it using SPECT computer simulations. Approach . The sine-amplitude method uses the time-varying aspect of the cardiac signal in ECG-gated SPECT studies to extract a component of the measured data that satisfies the eDCCs, even if the overall activity does not. Four noise-free activity distributions were simulated: a time-varying point source inside the heart, the point source with static liver activity, time-varying left-ventricle (LV) activity, and the LV with static liver activity. The liver activity violated the eDCC constraints. The method was evaluated with different levels of Poisson noise and liver activity. Consistency between exponential projections was assessed using the mean normalised difference (MND) over single- and multi-slice axial ranges. Main Results . In noise-free simulations, the liver activity outside the region of constant attenuation increased the LV activity single-slice MND fromto. For the eleven-slice range, the presence of liver increased the LV activity MND fromto. The sine-amplitude method reduced the LV single-slice MND toand the eleven-slice MND to. With noisy data, the sine-amplitude method improved the average MND values for all tested liver levels when the total heart counts were 2.1-53 times a typical clinical acquisition, depending on the axial range. Significance. For time-varying SPECT data, the sine-amplitude approach can broaden the applicability of exponential data consistency conditions in non-homogeneous attenuation.

title: Towards artificial intelligence based preoperative dosimetry for liver 90 Y selective internal radiation therapy.
abstract: Objective. Selective internal radiation therapy delivers Y-90 microspheres through the hepatic arterial system to achieve tumoricidal absorbed dose while limiting normal-tissue irradiation. Current pre-treatment dosimetry requires angiography and 99 mTc-MAA imaging, resulting in an invasive and resource-intensive workflow. This study evaluates the feasibility of estimating post-therapy Y-90 dose distribution directly from diagnostic multiphasic CT using an automated deep-learning pipeline, without requiring angiography or surrogate-particle imaging. Approach. In 152 treatments from the multicenter PROACTIF registry, arterial- and portal-phase CT, together with clinically documented perfusion territories and injected activities, were processed through automated segmentation, rigid registration, differential CT generation, and a generative model synthesizing a PET-like Y-90 activity map. Absorbed-dose maps were computed using the Local Dose Deposition method, and predictive accuracy was assessed using tumor dose-volume metrics and voxelwise spatial agreement. Main results. For the best-performing configuration, the median tumor D70 error was 23 Gy, with substantial inter-patient variability reflecting the challenges of CT-only dose prediction. High-dose coverage (V200) showed a similar pattern. In contrast, spatial agreement was consistently strong, with perfused-volume gamma passing rates around 93% and tumor-level rates around 85%, indicating that the macro-scale distribution of microspheres can be approximated from diagnostic CT. The full pipeline was fully automated and produced predictive dosimetry in under 30 S. Significance. Pre-angiography CT contains exploitable information about arterial enhancement and perfusion patterns that enables feasible CT-only prediction of Y-90 spatial distribution. While tumor-level absorbed-dose metrics remain variable, the strong spatial agreement suggests potential utility as an early planning tool to support patient selection or guide catheterization strategy prior to angiography.

title: An imaging framework for nuclei-based three-dimensional cell quantification in intact tissue using phase-contrast x-ray CT.
abstract: Objective. Quantitative analysis of cellular morphology and spatial organisation within intact tissue remains challenging, particularly when three-dimensional information must be preserved. This study investigates whether laboratory propagation-based phase-contrast x-ray computed tomography (CT) can support nuclei-based quantitative analysis in unstained tissue while retaining the surrounding tissue architecture. Approach. We propose a nuclei-based quantitative imaging workflow that combines laboratory propagation-based phase-contrast x-ray CT with volumetric segmentation. Intact unstained liver tissue was imaged at cellular resolution, then nuclei were segmented throughout the reconstructed volume and quantitative metrics describing the nuclear morphology and spatial organisation were extracted. The resulting measurements were evaluated in two non-overlapping volumes of interest and compared with histological reference data using thickness-matched virtual CT slices. Main results. The proposed workflow enabled visualisation and segmentation of individual nuclei throughout intact unstained liver tissue. Comparable nuclear morphology and spatial organisation metrics were obtained from two non-overlapping volumes of interest, indicating stable segmentation performance within the analysed specimen. Comparison with H&E histology demonstrated broad agreement in nuclear morphology. Significance. This work demonstrates the feasibility of nuclei-based quantitative analysis using laboratory phase-contrast x-ray CT in intact unstained tissue. The approach provides volumetric cellular information while preserving tissue architecture and may complement conventional histological assessment in applications requiring three-dimensional analysis. These findings highlight the potential of laboratory phase-contrast CT for quantitative tissue characterisation and spatial cellular analysis.

title: Decay-time correction for dual-panel in-beam PET monitoring of carbon-ion SOBP irradiation.
abstract: Objective. In-beam positron emission tomography (PET) is a promising technique for monitoring beam range and activity distribution in carbon-ion radiotherapy. However, spread-out Bragg peak (SOBP) delivery introduces a challenge because sequentially delivered energy layers experience different decay times in-beam and off-beam PET acquisitions. This study developed a decay-time correction method to reduce temporal bias in measured PET activity distributions under SOBP irradiation. Approach. A dual-panel LYSO-SiPM PET system in a 4 × 1 module arrangement, with an effective detection area of 21.28 × 5.32 cm 2 , was used to acquire in-beam and off-beam PET images during homogeneous solid-water phantom irradiation. The beam was delivered in scanning mode using sequential high-to-low energy layers, with up to 11 layers ranging from 216.50-263.23 MeV u -1 . Four irradiation schemes were evaluated: physical-dose, relative biological effectiveness-weighted dose (RWD), full-opposing-field RWD, and half-opposing-field RWD SOBP. A Monte Carlo-based decay-time correction framework was established by incorporating beam delivery timing, radionuclide decay characteristics, and activity accumulation. Corrected PET images were compared with Monte Carlo-simulated activity distributions generated using a platform consistent with the experimental setup. Main Results. Sequential energy-layer delivery and radionuclide decay affected measured PET activity distributions under SOBP irradiation. After correction, experimental PET profiles showed improved agreement with corresponding Monte Carlo profiles across all four SOBP schemes. Depending on the irradiation scheme and acquisition mode, the correction reduced root-mean-square error by approximately 7.1%-73.1%, reduced SOBP-region mean absolute deviation by approximately 7.0%-72.2%, and increased the Pearson correlation coefficient from 0.861-0.973 before correction to 0.947-0.980 after correction. Significance. This study addressed temporal bias in PET activity distributions caused by decay-time differences among sequentially delivered energy layers during carbon-ion SOBP irradiation. The proposed correction improved the reliability and interpretability of dual-panel in-beam PET under sequential multi-energy carbon-ion irradiation, extending planar PET monitoring toward more treatment-relevant verification scenarios.

title: Comparison of proton, helium-ion, and carbon-ion CT imaging for hadron radiotherapy using Monte Carlo simulations.
abstract: Objective To perform a comprehensive comparative analysis of proton, helium-ion, and carbon-ion computed tomography (CT) as direct imaging modalities for hadron therapy treatment planning, focusing on Relative Stopping Power (RSP) reconstruction accuracy and patient radiation dose. Approach: High-fidelity Monte Carlo simulations were conducted using the GATE/Geant4 platform to model a standard CTP404 phantom. RSP maps were reconstructed using two iterative algorithms: the Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (SART) and the Richardson-Lucy (RL) deconvolution. Imaging performance was evaluated by comparing reconstructed RSP values against ground truth data for various tissue-equivalent inserts, while integral doses were estimated for a human head geometry using a Shepp-Logan-like phantom. Main results: All investigated particle modalities demonstrated a significant dose reduction compared to conventional X-ray CT protocols (which are approximately 40 mGy). The estimated imaging doses were 0.5 mGy for protons, 1.3 mGy for helium ions, and 7.5 mGy for carbon ions. In terms of accuracy, carbon-ion imaging achieved promising accuracy for soft-tissue materials (mean absolute error <0.5%). Helium ions offered a balanced performance with sub-1% errors for most materials and a dose burden significantly lower than carbon ions. Protons exhibited the widest range of RSP deviations. Significance: Direct particle imaging eliminates the systematic uncertainties inherent in photon-to-hadron conversion, which typically introduce RSP deviations of 1.6%-3.5% in standard single-energy X-ray CT. While carbon ions provide better RSP reconstruction precision essential for complex treatment plans in heterogeneous anatomy, helium and proton imaging offer exceptional dose sparing, making them particularly advantageous for pediatric patients and frequent adaptive replanning scenarios.

title: Impact of depth-of-interaction and spatially-variant point-spread-function model on the performance of ultra-high resolution brain PET.
abstract: Objective. To implement a spatially-variant point spread function (VarPSF) model for the NeuroEXPLORER (NX) brain positron emission tomography (PET) scanner in the open-source Yale Reconstruction Toolkit for PET, and investigate the interplay between depth-of-interaction (DOI) resolution and resolution modeling. Approach. PSF parameters were estimated from simulated and physically measured point sources. Three primary DOI configurations were evaluated: eight-layer DOI (8DOI), two-layer DOI (2DOI), and no DOI (noDOI), with an additional 4DOI comparison in the off-center simulated Derenzo study. Reconstructions using VarPSF, a spatially-invariant PSF measured at the field-of-view center (SinglePSF), and no PSF modeling (noPSF) were assessed using simulated Derenzo and brain phantoms, a physical Derenzo phantom, and one non-human primate (NHP) scan. Main results. In simulated and physical Derenzo studies, VarPSF yielded higher peak-to-valley ratios than SinglePSF and noPSF at the final evaluated iterations, with pronounced gains at large radial offsets. title: AnF-DiffPET: anatomy- and frequency-guided diffusion for simulated low-dose PET/CT denoising.
abstract: Objective. Positron emission tomography (PET) provides essential functional information for disease assessment. However, reducing injected activity or acquisition time produces low-dose (LD) PET with stronger count-dependent noise and less reliable uptake quantification. Diffusion models offer a promising solution for PET denoising by progressively recovering high-dose (HD) PET images from LD inputs. However, LD-to-HD PET denoising remains challenging because of limited anatomical guidance, unstable multi-scale feature propagation, and inaccurate recovery of uptake patterns in the frequency domain. Approach. We propose AnF-DiffPET, an anatomy- and frequency-guided diffusion framework for computed tomography (CT)-conditioned LD PET denoising. The framework integrates anatomical-frequency guidance, Multi-Scale Cross-Transformer Reconstruction, and Frequency-Contrastive Hard Mining to enhance anatomy-aware feature modulation and frequency-domain consistency during denoising. Main results. Experimental results across four simulated LD PET/CT datasets show that the proposed method improves image fidelity, anatomical consistency, and quantitative fidelity over representative CNN-based, GAN-based, Transformer-based, Mamba-based, and diffusion-based methods. Significance. AnF-DiffPET provides a PET/CT-specific diffusion restoration framework that combines anatomical guidance, multi-scale feature reconstruction, and frequency-domain regularization for LD PET denoising. The code and trained models will be publicly released upon acceptance.

title: X-ray projection-guided deformation vector field estimation and dynamic CBCT imaging using patient-specific vector-quantized diffusion.
abstract: Objective. To develop a conditional vector-quantized (VQ) diffusion-based dynamic cone beam computed tomography imaging framework using dual-view x-ray projections for accurate reconstruction of respiratory-induced lung tumor motion, with the potential to enable four-dimensional (4D) target verification during lung radiotherapy. Methods. Patient-specific respiratory motion models were constructed from planning 4D- computed tomography(CT) images using deformable image registration and principal component analysis (PCA). Synthetic DVFs were generated by sampling PCA coefficients and applied to the reference-phase CT images to produce dynamic three-dimensional (3D) volumes, from which paired dual-view DRRs were generated. A conditional VQ diffusion framework was developed, consisting of separate two-dimensional and 3D vector quantized variational autoencoder s for encoding DRRs and DVFs into discrete latent representations, followed by a conditional diffusion model to learn the mapping from x-ray projection features to deformation vector field (DVF) latent representations. During inference, dual-view x-ray projections were encoded and processed by the conditional diffusion model to estimate DVFs, which were then used to deform the reference CT image and reconstruct temporally resolved 3D volumes. Results. The simulation study demonstrates that the estimated DVFs effectively captured the respiratory-induced deformation of lung tumors, and the reconstructed dynamic volume CT images demonstrated accurate anatomical motion characteristics across respiratory phases. Conclusion. The proposed patient-specific VQ diffusion framework enables accurate estimation of respiratory-induced lung tumor motion from dual-view x-ray projections and facilitates the high-temporal-resolution dynamic volume CT reconstruction. The results demonstrate its potential as an image-guided solution for tumor motion tracking in lung tumor radiotherapy.

title: Generative modeling of complex-valued brain MRI data.
abstract: Objective. Standard magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reconstruction pipelines discard phase information captured during acquisition, despite its sensitivity to tissue properties that are not represented by magnitude alone. The aim of this study is to develop a generative framework that jointly models magnitude and phase information in complex-valued brain MRI data and enables the conditional generation of MRI samples representing normal and abnormal brain tissue. Approach. The proposed generative framework combines a conditional variational autoencoder, which compresses complex-valued MRI scans into latent representations while preserving phase coherence, with a flow-matching-based generative model. Synthetic sample quality is assessed using a real-versus-synthetic classifier, image-space coverage tests, and downstream classifiers trained on synthetic data for abnormal tissue detection. Main results. The autoencoder preserves phase coherence above 0.997. Real-vs-synthetic classifiers yielded low AUROCs between 0.53 and 0.64 for generated phase images supporting realistic phase modeling. Magnitude was moderately distinguishable, with AUROCs between 0.53 and 0.82, suggesting appreciable overlap between real and synthetic sample distributions while also indicating a distribution shift for several sequences. Image-space coverage was broad. On the held-out test split, no consistent directional difference from the matched real-to-real references was detected in any evaluated setting, while the training split showed slight to moderate undercoverage depending on acquisition sequence and tissue condition. In downstream normal-versus-abnormal classification, classifiers trained entirely on synthetic data achieve an AUROC of 0.880, surpassing the real-data baseline of 0.842 on the fastMRI dataset. This advantage persists on an independent external test set with biopsy-confirmed labels. Significance. The proposed framework demonstrates the feasibility of jointly modeling magnitude and phase information for normal and abnormal complex-valued brain MRI data. Beyond synthetic data generation, the framework enables future investigation of how magnitude and phase jointly encode pathology-specific features once sufficiently large raw MRI datasets with fine-grained, pathology-confirmed labels become available.

title: A wavelet-guided diffusion method for brain magnetic resonance parameter mapping using MOLED-based datasets: proof-of-principle.
abstract: Objective. Quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (qMRI) can noninvasively acquire parametric maps, providing quantitative biomarkers for clinical assessment. Parametric maps, such as T 2 , T 2 * , and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), characterize distinct biophysical processes in tissue in an interpretable, numerical manner. Owing to their distinct physical origins, various parametric maps differ in physical units, numerical magnitudes, and dynamic ranges. Even for the same type of parametric map, inter-subject differences may still exist in anatomical morphology, tissue characteristics, and the local distributions of parameter values. However, deep learning methods trained in image-domain directly learn pixel-level parameter values, and variations in numerical scales and subject-specific parameter distributions may result in anatomical detail loss and localized artifacts in certain tasks. To address this challenge and to deliver dependable quantitative references for clinical assessment, we propose a wavelet-guided diffusion method. Approach. We extend the discrete convolution wavelet transform (DCWT) to two dimensions and combine it with a conditional denoising diffusion method to develop a diffusion-based DCWT (Diff-DCWT) for parameter mapping. Diff-DCWT achieves accurate parameter mapping under the guidance of wavelet coefficient maps, thereby reducing reliance on image domain learning. The performance of Diff-DCWT is evaluated through simulation and in vivo experiments across T 2 , T 2 * , and ADC mapping tasks. Main Results. Both simulation and healthy volunteer experiments demonstrate that T 2 , T 2 * , and ADC maps obtained from Diff-DCWT maintain excellent visual quality and quantitative accuracy. Clinical case studies suggest the potential utility of Diff-DCWT-derived T 2 and ADC maps for stroke staging and help distinguish lesional from normal brain regions in glioma. Significance. Diff-DCWT establishes a high-fidelity framework for parameter mapping and exhibits preliminary clinical value in stroke staging and glioma characterization. Moreover, this work demonstrates the potential of wavelet-domain prior guidance for deep learning-based qMRI applications.

title: Learned proximal gradient flow matching for limited-angle CT reconstruction.
abstract: Objective The primary objective of this research is to address the challenges of limited-angle computed tomography (CT) reconstruction that arises when projection data are acquired over an angular range smaller than that required for theoretically exact reconstruction. This ill-posed problem leads to severe artifacts compromising diagnostic quality. The study aims to develop a robust and efficient framework to achieve high-fidelity image reconstruction. Approach: The proposed method, termed Learned Proximal Gradient Flow Matching (LPGFM), introduces a novel framework that synergistically combines explicit optimization principles with deep generative models. Secondly, a proximal correction step enforces strict data consistency, enhancing robustness against deviations. title: Smooth total variation regularization for interference detection and elimination (STRIDE) for MRI.
abstract: Objective. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is increasingly required to operate near electronic devices that emit dynamic electromagnetic interference (EMI). Existing reference-channel EMI removal methods estimate a transfer function between EMI sensors and imaging coils from the measured data alone, and do not use prior knowledge about the structure of MR images. We develop and validate an EMI removal method that uses the inherent spatial smoothness of MR images as an additional prior, demonstrated on a head-only 0.5 T scanner. Approach. Smooth total variation regularization for interference detection and elimination (STRIDE) operates in the image domain. For each image column, EMI sensor data are combined and subtracted from the imaging coil data such that the2 norm of the total variation (TV) along the readout direction is minimized. This exploits the smoothness of MR images, a property well-known in compressed sensing but not previously used in EMI removal. STRIDE was evaluated on phantom and in-vivo brain datasets under EMI scenarios replicating sources encountered at our affiliated hospitals, and compared against two implementations of External Dynamic Interference Estimation and Removal (EDITER). Main results. STRIDE produced visually better EMI removal and generally higher temporal signal-to-noise ratio than both EDITER implementations, with comparable EMI removal percentage. STRIDE also resulted in lower or equal root-mean-square error than both EDITER implementations in all 8 phantom EMI conditions tested. These results held across both phantom and in-vivo datasets. Significance. STRIDE shows that incorporating known properties of MR images into the EMI removal problem provides meaningful improvements over methods that rely on measured data alone. The approach is deterministic, training-free, sequence-independent, and compatible with existing EMI sensor hardware. STRIDE therefore extends reference-channel EMI removal to scenarios where existing methods fail, particularly point-of-care and interventional MRI outside fully shielded environments, providing a deterministic, training-free alternative to machine-learning approaches.

title: Domain-aligned self-supervision: CT-specialized DINOv3 enhances PET/CT tumor segmentation.
abstract: Objective. This study investigates how domain-aligned self-supervised pretraining influences downstream PET/CT tumor segmentation, with a focus on disentangling the roles of domain proximity and pretraining dataset scale. Approach. We compared nnU-Net segmentation models initialized from random weights or from DINOv3 encoders pretrained on natural images, x-ray mammography, CT, or PET, using datasets of different sizes. To disentangle the effects of pretraining domain and dataset size, CT-DINOv3 encoders were pretrained using different numbers of 2D CT slices, including subsets matched in size to the pretraining datasets from other domains. Models were evaluated on two PET/CT benchmarks, autoPET (whole-body, FDG/prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)) and HECKTOR (head-and-neck primary tumors and metastatic lymph nodes), using five-fold cross-validation with frozen encoders. Main results. CT-pretrained models achieved the highest Dice scores for lymph nodes, FDG lesions, and PSMA lesions. For primary tumors, PET pretraining produced the highest observed Dice score, followed by CT pretraining, suggesting the potential benefit of in-domain representations when PET data are sufficient. Notably, PET pretraining exceeded size-matched CT pretraining for PSMA but remained below models pretrained on larger CT datasets for both PSMA and FDG targets. In contrast, natural-image pretraining did not outperform from-scratch training despite its much larger pretraining scale, indicating that scale alone is insufficient when domain proximity is low. Across comparisons, strong transfer reflected the combination of domain proximity and sufficient pretraining scale, especially for CT-based models with broad data availability. Significance. These results demonstrate that both domain proximity and dataset scale jointly determine the effectiveness of self-supervised pretraining. While higher domain alignment improves performance at comparable scale, sufficient data is required to realize this benefit. CT-based pretraining provides a favorable balance between domain relevance and data availability, leading to robust performance across tasks. This study provides practical guidance for selecting pretraining strategies in PET/CT segmentation.

title: ReCo-Diff: residual-conditioned deterministic sampling for cold diffusion in sparse-view CT.
abstract: Objective Sparse-view computed tomography (CT) reduces radiation dose and acquisition time but introduces structured streak artifacts that make reconstruction severely ill-posed. Cold-diffusion approaches can model such deterministic degradation processes, but existing sampling strategies may rely on scalar similarity criteria and predefined thresholds to trigger sample-adaptive resets of the degradation-level trajectory. We aim to replace this threshold-based sampling control with spatially resolved residual conditioning. Approach We propose ReCo-Diff, a residual-conditioned cold-diffusion framework for sparse-view CT reconstruction. At each reverse step, a zero-residual baseline prediction is re-degraded using the CT degradation operator, and the resulting signed image-domain re-degradation discrepancy is used as a spatial conditioning map for a second restoration pass. ReCo-Diff does not require an adaptive reset during residual-conditioned sampling and instead follows a predetermined degradation schedule. A one-time level transition is additionally used for highly sparse inputs. The method was evaluated on the AAPM Low-Dose CT dataset under 18-, 36-, and 72-view settings using a patient-wise split with one held-out test volume. Main results ReCo-Diff achieved PSNR values of 38.54, 42.57, and 46.98 dB at 18, 36, and 72 views, respectively. At 18 views, matched-computation analysis showed that ReCo-Diff achieved 38.54 dB compared with 38.25 dB for a two-pass zero-residual control under the same 18-NFE budget. A spatially shifted-residual control achieved 37.65 dB, indicating that effective residual conditioning benefits from spatial correspondence with the current degraded state. Significance. ReCo-Diff replaces adaptive trajectory control with step-wise spatial residual conditioning in deterministic cold diffusion. Matched-computation analysis shows that the reconstruction benefit depends on spatially aligned residual information rather than on the additional network evaluation alone. The proposed strategy provides an alternative approach to controlling error propagation under a predetermined degradation schedule without relying on sample-adaptive reset decisions.

title: A harmonisation framework for multi-centre preclinical PET imaging across a national research infrastructure.
abstract: Objective Quantitative preclinical positron emission tomography (PET) imaging plays an important role in translational research, yet variability across scanners, sites, and analysis workflows remains a major barrier to robust multi-centre studies. In this work, we developed and evaluated a harmonisation framework across a national network of preclinical PET facilities. Approach. Six identical NEMA NU~4-2008 image quality phantoms were manufactured and distributed to six sites, where they were imaged using local acquisition and reconstruction protocols across multiple scanner platforms. Main Results. Substantial variability in contrast recovery, uniformity, and spill-over ratios was observed under site-specific conditions. Centralised automated re-analysis produced only minor reductions in variability, indicating that inter-user effects were relatively small, compared to site-specific protocol variations. In contrast, optimisation of reconstruction parameters led to a marked reduction in inter-scanner variability (an average of 60\% reduction across larger rods), particularly for voxel-wise maximum contrast recovery coefficients (CRC_max^vox), which are more sensitive to noise and reconstruction settings than the standard axial averaging NEMA CRC metric. Following harmonisation, the variability of CRC_max^vox approached and was lower that of conventional axial-averaged NEMA analysis (CRC_max^avg), with reductions ranging 7--33\% across the 1--5 mm rods, demonstrating improved quantitative consistency even at the voxel level. Significance. These findings show that scanner and site-specific protocol variations are the dominant factors for harmonisation in preclinical PET. By systematically evaluating acquisition, image reconstruction and analysis related sources of variability across a national network of heterogeneous preclinical PET systems, this work provides a practical framework for harmonisation. The proposed framework is conceptually aligned with clinical harmonisation initiatives such as EARL and provides a practical basis for the future development of harmonised performance ranges across preclinical scanners. This enables more reliable multi-centre studies and supports the use of quantitative, voxel-wise imaging biomarkers in translational research.

title: High-fidelity 3D geometric reconstruction of pelvic organs from MRI: a hybrid deep learning and iterative optimization approach.
abstract: Objective The generation of high-fidelity, high-quality three-dimensional (3D) pelvic organ geometries from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived segmentation masks remains challenging. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a hybrid framework for reconstructing the bladder, uterus, and rectum, and to assess its geometric fidelity, mesh-quality proxy performance, and reconstruction efficiency. Approach. We developed a hybrid deformable shape modeling framework that integrates deep learning prediction with iterative optimization for the reconstruction of the bladder, uterus, and rectum. The framework consists of three core components: (1) a geometry-aware multi-level deep learning architecture that preserves topological consistency of pelvic organs; (2) a two-stage amortized optimization training strategy that balances global shape capture and local surface refinement; and (3) a holistic synergy mechanism-where iterative optimization provides supervision for deep learning during the training phase, and during inference, deep learning rapidly predicts the global organ morphology, followed by iterative optimization to refine local surfaces and mesh quality. Main results. Before iterative refinement, the proposed model outperformed representative deep learning-based reconstruction methods in geometric fidelity, achieving CD/DSC values of 5.5 × 10⁻³/0.788 for the bladder, 3.7 × 10⁻³/0.839 for the rectum, and 4.2 × 10⁻³/0.900 for the uterus. Deep learning-based initialization enabled the complete hybrid framework to converge within approximately 100 iterations, with a reconstruction time of approximately 35 s per organ on a CPU and 1.5 s on a GPU. At the patient level, the mean minSICN and minSIGE values of the 10 worst volumetric elements were 0.0807 and 0.0844, respectively, exceeding those achieved by traditional geometric post-processing methods. Significance. The proposed framework connects image-domain segmentation with structural-domain applications by efficiently generating high-fidelity, high-quality pelvic organ geometries with improved mesh-quality proxy performance. These geometries may support statistical shape assessment and may provide candidate surface representations for subsequent volumetric meshing and solver-specific biomechanical validation.

This study aimed to develop and evaluate a hybrid framework for reconstructing the bladder, uterus, and rectum, and to assess its geometric fidelity, mesh-quality proxy performance, and reconstruction efficiency. Approach. We developed a hybrid deformable shape modeling framework that integrates deep learning prediction with iterative optimization for the reconstruction of the bladder, uterus, and rectum. The framework consists of three core components: (1) a geometry-aware multi-level deep learning architecture that preserves topological consistency of pelvic organs; (2) a two-stage amortized optimization training strategy that balances global shape capture and local surface refinement; and (3) a holistic synergy mechanism-where iterative optimization provides supervision for deep learning during the training phase, and during inference, deep learning rapidly predicts the global organ morphology, followed by iterative optimization to refine local surfaces and mesh quality. Main results. Before iterative refinement, the proposed model outperformed representative deep learning-based reconstruction methods in geometric fidelity, achieving CD/DSC values of 5.5 × 10⁻³/0.788 for the bladder, 3.7 × 10⁻³/0.839 for the rectum, and 4.2 × 10⁻³/0.900 for the uterus. At the patient level, the mean minSICN and minSIGE values of the 10 worst volumetric elements were 0.0807 and 0.0844, respectively, exceeding those achieved by traditional geometric post-processing methods. Significance. The proposed framework connects image-domain segmentation with structural-domain applications by efficiently generating high-fidelity, high-quality pelvic organ geometries with improved mesh-quality proxy performance. title: Adaptive physics-inspired angular-spatial modeling for multi-shell diffusion MRI denoising.
abstract: Objective Multi-shell diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) provides rich q-space information but is susceptible to noise, which can disrupt spatial anatomy, intra-shell directional relationships, inter-shell signal attenuation, and downstream diffusion parameter estimation. We aim to develop a denoising method that jointly preserves spatial structure, directional information, and shell-specific signal characteristics. Approach We propose ASD-NCSM, an adaptive physics-inspired angular-spatial framework with a fixed three-stage alternating architecture. It combines intra-shell differential angular graph message passing with 2.5D spatial residual refinement. Noise-Conditioned Shell Modulation (NCSM) adaptively regulates angular updates according to b-value, spatial residual and angular dispersion proxies, and local gating. A Shell-wise Physical Attenuation and Angular Relation Consistency (SPARC) objective further constrains shell-wise signal fidelity, logarithmic attenuation, and local angular structure. The model was evaluated on HCP multi-shell dMRI with simulated noise and independently acquired real in vivo brain dMRI data. Main results Across five simulated noise levels from 2% to 10%, ASD-NCSM achieved the best overall DWI restoration among MPPCA, 1D-CNN, ECDM, SAN2N, and dMRI-Swin, with consistent subject-level advantages in PSNR, SSIM, and NRMSE. At 6% noise, principal-direction angular nRMSE was 32.68 ± 2.76%, with significant differences from all five baselines after Holm correction. ASD-NCSM also achieved the lowest mean MAE for FA, MD, AD, and RD, and the lowest relative MAE for ODI and FISO, while NDI was comparable to 1D-CNN and dMRI-Swin. For real data without noise-free references, Q-PEFT yielded the lowest angular cross-fit inconsistency (2.29 ± 0.10%) across three test subjects while maintaining limited signal and downstream-parameter changes. Significance ASD-NCSM jointly preserves spatial continuity, directional geometry, and shell-level attenuation, providing balanced signal recovery, directional preservation, and downstream parameter stability for multi-shell dMRI denoising.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
abstract: Objective Limited-angle cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is attractive for imageguided radiotherapy and imaging-guided procedure when full-arc acquisition is impractical, but the incomplete angular sampling leads to severe streaking, shading, and structural distortion. This study aimed to develop a physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction framework for recovering anatomically faithful volumetric CBCT from limited-angle projections. Approach: We propose PCGA-Net, a dual-domain reconstruction framework that combines projection completion, analytic geometric reconstruction, and image-domain refinement within a unified cross-domain design. Specifically, a projection completion module first estimates missingangle information from the measured limited-angle projections. A geometry-aware reconstruction module then maps the completed projections into image space using differentiable cone-beam forward and backward-projection operators. Finally, a volumetric refinement module suppresses residual artifacts and restores anatomical detail under geometry-guided cross-domain consistency supervision. The framework was evaluated on three cohorts: gynecologic highdose-rate brachytherapy, abdominal liver 4DCT, and head-and-neck CBCT. Main Results: Across all three cohorts, PCGA-Net consistently outperformed conventional limitedangle FDK reconstruction and the compared learning-based baselines, cGAN and PatRecon-Net, in both qualitative and quantitative evaluation. On the gynecologic HDR brachytherapy cohort, PCGA-Net achieved an MAE of 34.47 ± 6.28 HU, an SSIM of 0.87 ± 0.04, and a PSNR of 35.79 ± 0.95 dB. On the abdominal liver 4DCT cohort, PCGA-Net achieved 39.27 ± 6.10 HU MAE, 0.82 ± 0.03 SSIM, and 36.85 ± 1.16 dB PSNR.On the head-and-neck CBCT cohort, PCGA-Net achieved 28.42 ± 4.88 HU MAE, 0.91 ± 0.05 SSIM, and 38.52 ± 0.95 dB PSNR. In all three cohorts, PCGA-Net exceeded cGAN and PatRecon-Net across all evaluated metrics. Significance: These results indicate that jointly enforcing projection-domain completion, analytic imaging geometry, and image-domain refinement is an effective strategy for limited-angle CBCT reconstruction. PCGA-Net provides a robust short-arc reconstruction framework across multiple anatomical sites, supporting its potential utility in constrained imageguided therapeutic and procedural settings.

title: Nonlinear stability phenotypes and collapse dynamics of multi-organ radiomics in total-body PET imaging: toward digital twin-oriented robustness assessment.
abstract: Objective Radiomics analysis in PET offers a high-dimensional representation of tissue characteristics, yet its reliability is limited by sensitivity to acquisition perturbations, particularly dose reduction. This study aims to introduce a nonlinear stability phenotyping framework to characterize dose-response behavior of multi-organ radiomics and evaluate their potential relevance for future digital twin-oriented applications. Approach: A multi-center dataset of 550 total-body PET scans was analyzed. Dose reduction was simulated using list-mode subsampling (dose reduction factor - DRF = 2-100). A total of 107 radiomics features were extracted per organ. Stability was quantified using Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) and summarized as stability fractions. Nonlinear models were fitted to organ- and feature-level trajectories. Stability phenotypes and critical thresholds were derived, along with organ-level instability metrics. Main results: Radiomics stability exhibited strongly nonlinear, organ-dependent behavior. Feature-level analysis identified frequent sigmoid-associated collapse patterns with high descriptive model fits (R²>0.90). The liver showed the highest instability burden (30.8% unstable features), followed by esophagus and kidneys (18-20%). Texture features were the primary source of instability, whereas shape features remained robust. Organ-level trajectories demonstrated heterogeneous responses, with some organs maintaining high stability (0.80-0.95) across DRFs, while others showed sharp declines (down to 0.64). Linear (stable) behavior dominated at the organ level, though masking underlying nonlinear feature dynamics. Significance: Radiomics stability in total-body PET follows nonlinear, phenotype-driven dynamics with identifiable tipping points and organ-specific sensitivity. The proposed framework provides a behavior-based approach for evaluating radiomics robustness and supports the selection of reliable features and organs for robust quantitative imaging and may inform future digital twin-oriented applications.

title: Spot-wise compensation of proton beam deflection and radiation field deformation in the transverse magnetic field of an in-beam MR scanner using a research version of a commercial treatment planning system.
abstract: Objective Magnetic resonance-integrated proton therapy (MRiPT) offers the potential for high-precision, image-guided particle therapy but is challenged by magnetic field (MF)-induced proton beam deflection and radiation field deformation. Unless compensated for, these effects compromise dose conformity and prohibit clinical implementation. This work aims to develop and experimentally validate a spot-wise compensation method capable of restoring proton dose distributions in the presence of a measured 3D magnetic vector field map within a clinical treatment planning system (TPS). Approach A spot-wise compensation framework was implemented in a research version of RayStation, a TPS commercially available for clinical use. The method compensates both lateral beam deflection and MF-induced radiation field deformation by shifting individual pencil-beam spots based on displacement vectors derived from dose calculations in water phantoms using the measured MF of an in-beam MR scanner integrated with a horizontal proton beamline. Two complementary strategies were implemented: a patient-specific approach based on plan-specific displacement calculations, and a generic approach using precomputed displacement maps derived from a reference phantom. Compensation performance was evaluated in representative clinical cases. Dose distributions were experimentally validated using 2D ionisation chamber array measurements. Main Results Both compensation methods effectively restored target coverage, dose homogeneity, and organ-at-risk sparing to the level of no-MF reference plans. The patient-specific method generally achieved a higher performance, whereas the generic compensation method enabled rapid automated correction with sufficient accuracy for clinical workflows involving deep-seated tumours. Local γ-analysis demonstrated excellent agreement between measured and calculated doses, with pass rates exceeding 98.5% for 3%/3 mm criteria. Significance This work demonstrates that compensation of MF-induced proton beam deflection and field deformation can be achieved entirely within a research version of the RayStation TPS using measured, MR scanner-specific MF data. The proposed method provides a scalable, robust framework for future MRiPT clinical applications.&#xD.

title: Silver sodium nitroprusside nano-aggregates for ultrasound-activated immunomodulatory therapy of MRSA pneumonia.
abstract: The clinical management of methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) pneumonia is hindered by biofilm infections and cytokine storms. A key challenge is the lack of real-time monitoring tools for the inflammatory microenvironment during treatment. In this study, we developed a theranostic platform (CS@EAgNP) using TPP-modified chitosan to load silver sodium nitroprusside nano-aggregates (AgNP) and epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG). This system combines ultrasound (US) imaging with US-activated therapy. The CS@EAgNP nano-aggregates can act as an excellent US contrast enhancer. In vivo US imaging indicated that AgNP generated significantly enhanced echo signals at the infection site, providing real-time and high-contrast visualization of the inflammatory foci that was unattainable with normal lung tissue. Moreover, these nano-aggregates release NO, silver and EGCG under US. The NO and silver penetrate biofilms to kill MRSA, while EGCG scavenges reactive oxygen species and modulates inflammation. This reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines like IL-6 and TNF- α , mitigating the cytokine storm. In vivo results further confirm that this image-guided strategy achieves significant bacterial clearance and promotes lung tissue regeneration without detectable toxicity to major organs. This integrated approach bridges diagnosis and treatment, offering a promising solution for managing MRSA pneumonia.

title: Pre-clinical evaluation of a smartphone-assisted navigation system for surgical pin positioning in total knee arthroplasty.
abstract: Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) success is highly dependent on accurate implant alignment, however, 80% of procedures globally are performed manually. Manual procedures have higher alignment errors compared to robotic platforms and patient-specific instrumentation, yet these have limitations of high cost and intraoperative inflexibility, respectively. This study aimed to evaluate the intraoperative pin positioning accuracy and flexibility of a smartphone-assisted navigation system using CT-derived surgical plans. Three participants used the navigation system to perform 108 guide pin insertions (54 femoral, 54 tibial) on surrogate bone models based on CT-derived surgical plans. Testing included both default mechanical axis targets (0°) and user-selected navigated targets ranging from -3° to 3°. Accuracy was assessed by comparing achieved pin trajectories with the preoperative surgical plan. Median absolute angular deviations achieved ranged from 0.9° to 1.6° across all component-plane combinations, with an overall median deviation of 1.3° (IQR 0.6-2.1°). The proportion of insertions within a predefined ±3° clinical accuracy threshold ranged from 83.3% to 100%, and all component-plane combinations demonstrated deviations significantly within this threshold (p < 0.00001). These findings support the technical feasibility of the smartphone-assisted navigation system for surgical pin positioning under controlled pre-clinical conditions. Further studies will evaluate the navigation system in cadaveric models with experienced orthopaedic surgeon participants.

title: A Practical Pipeline for Patient-Specific Musculoskeletal Modeling: A Comprehensive MRI-Based Framework.
abstract: Patient-specific musculoskeletal (MS) modeling can provide estimates of internal joint loading that canot be measured directly. However, limitations in automated segmentation due to data-scarce environments, morphing difficulty caused by anatomical variability, and functional non-alignment are major bottlenecks that hinder the practical application of modeling and reduce productivity in musculoskeletal research. To comprehensively address these practical issues, this study proposes and validates an integrated, automated modeling framework.. First, we automatically segmented the lower extremity bones of the 4 knee osteoarthritis patients using a multi-atlas-based segmentation algorithm. By integrating the segmented bone with motion capture and force plate data, a modeling pipeline including multi-stage morphing and functional alignment processes was implemented. Using the constructed customized model, the medial and lateral knee contact forces (FMC and FLC) were estimated during a single-leg step-up exercise, and these were compared and evaluated against the results based on manual segmentation. The contact forces estimated through the automated segmentation framework demonstrated high consistency with the manual results. The mean absolute error ranged from 0.04 ± 0.03 to 0.06 ± 0.03 BW for FMC, and from 0.06 ± 0.04 to 0.09 ± 0.07 BW for FLC, and the intraclass correlation coefficient demonstrated a high correlation of over 0.99 across all patients. This study demonstrated that the proposed automated pipeline provides a practical approach to address misalignment caused by anatomical variability, while generating joint load estimates equivalent to the manual approach. By addressing key methodological challenges, this study will bring patient-specific models closer to future clinical application, where they could help assess individual loading across different activities and inform treatment and rehabilitation strategies.

title: A compact teacher-student knowledge-distillation framework for lumbar MRI segmentation.
abstract: Accurate segmentation of lumbar magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is important for quantitative assessment of degenerative spine disease, but it remains challenging because spinal structures show low contrast, variable morphology, and severe pixel-class imbalance. This study evaluates a compact teacher-student knowledge-distillation framework for multi-class lumbar MRI segmentation. The student network integrates a Res2Net encoder-decoder, a lightweight transformer bottleneck, and deep supervision; a manifold-constrained hyper-skip (MHC) module is evaluated as an optional constrained skip-fusion variant rather than assumed to be the sole source of improvement. A UNet++ teacher transfers soft probability, class-focused, and boundary-weighted information to guide boundary-sensitive anatomical regions. Under five-fold case-level GroupKFold validation on the primary public axial lumbar MRI dataset, the MHC full-KD variant achieved Dice 0.9141 ± 0.0021, foreground Dice 0.8934 ± 0.0026, IoU 0.8519 ± 0.0033, and HD95 3.1451 ± 0.2101. A no-MHC student trained with the same full distillation objective achieved essentially the same Dice (0.9141 ± 0.0021) with lower HD95 and lower measured latency, indicating that the full distillation objective, rather than the MHC block alone, explained most of the performance recovery toward the teacher. Replication on the 2026 Medical Lumbar Spine 3D Axial MRI Dataset achieved Dice 0.8960 ± 0.0032 and IoU 0.8224 ± 0.0047. A fixed label-harmonized train-on-primary/test-on-2026 transfer stress test achieved macro Dice 0.7002 ± 0.0181 and foreground Dice 0.6280 ± 0.0225. The results suggest that compact class-aware distillation can support reproducible lumbar MRI segmentation for future computer-aided measurement pipelines, while prospective and strict cross-institutional validation remain necessary.

title: 3D ViT network with selective feature enhancement and cross-dimensional interaction for colorectal T-stage classification in CT images.
abstract: Background. Obstructive colorectal cancer (OCC) often manifests on computed tomography (CT) as highly variable in morphology and location, with indistinct margins, atypical infiltration signs, and frequent adherence to surrounding structures. In addition, motion artifacts caused by intestinal peristalsis further degrade image quality and interfere with the identification of subtle structures. These factors readily lead to misassessment in T-stage evaluation, and accurately distinguishing between T4 and non-T4 stages is critical as it directly influences surgical planning and clinical decision-making. Purpose. To address challenges of imaging heterogeneity and motion artifacts in T-stage evaluation, we proposed a 3D vision transformer (ViT) based model with feature enhancement and cross-dimensional interaction for T4/non-T4 classification of OCC. Methods. First, we extended ViT into 3D and incorporate a selective feature enhancement module. This module computes attention weights based on feature means, adaptively enhancing discriminative information while suppressing redundant responses. It effectively mitigates difficulties in identifying subtle structures like serosal invasion caused by motion artifacts and low contrast in CT images, enabling the model to focus on diagnostically critical regions. Second, we introduced a cross-dimensional adaptive feature aggregation mechanism that established multi-scale 3D spatial dependencies, integrating global context with fine-grained local details. This significantly improves the model's ability to characterize tumors with complex and variable morphological features, thereby reducing staging inaccuracies due to underutilized spatial information. Furthermore, cross-domain knowledge transfer was employed to enrich the model's representational capacity and alleviate the inherent data scarcity in 3D medical image analysis. Results. Evaluated on a private dataset of 127 CT scans, the proposed model achieved an AUC of 0.8917 and an accuracy of 0.7917 in T4/non-T4 classification, significantly outperforming mainstream 3D medical image classification networks. Conclusions. Our approach offers clinicians a reliable decision support tool for accurate OCC staging, allowing surgeons to tailor operative strategies based on quantitatively reliable imaging assessments.
